stories.title: Amit's Earthquake Experience
stories.description: Amit recounts volunteering after the Latur earthquake in college. He initially felt anger at a shopkeeper charging high prices for essentials, but later realized that these high prices were necessary signals to incentivize more supply to reach the disaster zone.

stories.title: Putin's Energy Blackmail
stories.description: Ajay discusses how Putin cut off gas to Europe, expecting them to freeze. Instead of price controls, Europe allowed prices to rise. This reduced demand (factories switched fuels) and surged supply (LNG from US/Qatar), solving the crisis. Governments used direct subsidies to help the poor, preserving the price signal.

stories.title: The Uber Surge Pricing Lesson
stories.description: Amit uses Uber surge pricing to explain how prices work. He shares a story of a friend who missed a flight in Delhi because a government price cap on Ubers caused a shortage, meaning no cars were available regardless of willingness to pay.

stories.title: Cement and Steel Control
stories.description: Ajay shares a story from a journalist friend about the 1980s decontrol of cement and steel prices in India. Bureaucrats in the ministry felt a sense of personal catastrophe and loss of purpose because they could no longer control the allocation of these resources.

stories.title: Rent Control in Marine Drive
stories.description: Amit points to the dilapidated buildings on Marine Drive in Mumbai as a visual consequence of rent control. Landlords have no incentive to maintain properties when rents are frozen at 1940s levels, leading to a 'bombed-out' look.

recommendations.item: The Use of Knowledge in Society
recommendations.comment: Amit and Ajay discuss Friedrich Hayek's seminal paper, which explains how the price system coordinates dispersed knowledge in society better than any central planner could.
Amit recommends Leonard Read's essay, which illustrates the miracle of the price system through the creation of a humble pencil.
Ajay recommends Brad DeLong's book for a structural understanding of the economic policy consensus that created modern prosperity.
Ajay recommends Milton Friedman's classic textbook, stating that 'some things are just done right by the old masters'.
Amit recommends Michael Shellenberger's book to understand how well-intentioned policies like rent control ruined San Francisco.
Amit recommends Hernando de Soto's book in the context of property rights and how rent control is a form of theft.
Amit recommends Thomas Leonard's book, which argues that minimum wage laws were originally intended to exclude minorities from the workforce.
Amit recommends this article by Ajay Shah.

core_ideas.description: Prices are not just numbers; they are a communication system. High prices signal scarcity (information) and encourage producers to make more (incentive), while low prices signal abundance.

Interfering with prices (caps, floors, rent control) breaks the communication mechanism. It leads to shortages, black markets, and a misallocation of resources, hurting the very people it aims to help.
The economy is a complex system that organizes itself through the decentralized actions of millions of people guided by prices. No central planner can replicate this 'resource allocation'.

Societies forget the hard-learned lessons of the past (like the failures of socialism or price controls) as new generations grow up taking prosperity for granted. This leads to repeating old mistakes.
True progress comes from structural reforms (fixing the market engine) rather than parametric reforms (tweaking knobs like minimum wage or subsidies).

jokes_and_cultural_references.context: Amit jokes that 'slouching' is a physical problem of gravity, while 'utopia' is a disease of the mind.
Amit riffs on a Bengali slogan, translating it to 'We must become OECD'.
Amit shares a 'mondegreen' (misheard lyric) from the movie Gharonda, where he thought the song was about searching for tapioca pearls (Sabudana) instead of grain/livelihood (Abodana).
Amit quotes the classic line: 'We must do something. This is something. Let's do it.'
